query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a thin, oxide-forming element coating, such as Al, can improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.intervention: Addition of a thin, oxide-forming element coating, such as Al
generation.conditions: Temperature: 800 °C, Atmosphere: Air, Exposure-time: 5 h, Loading: No external loading
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer
generation.mechanism: The oxide-forming element coating reacts with oxygen to form a protective layer, preventing the underlying alloy from reacting with oxygen and reducing oxidation
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxygen resistance, reduced oxidation, and potentially improved high-temperature mechanical properties
generation.boundary: Temperature: 800 °C, Atmosphere: Air, Exposure-time: 5 h, Loading: No external loading
generation.uncertainty: The effectiveness of the oxide-forming element coating in improving oxygen resistance, the optimal coating thickness and composition, and the potential impact on mechanical properties

falsification_experiment.design: Expose coated and uncoated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr samples to air at 800 °C for 5 h, then evaluate oxidation resistance and mechanical properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated sample shows no significant improvement in oxidation resistance or mechanical properties compared to the uncoated sample, the hypothesis is falsified

A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

How 10 at% Al Addition in the Ti-V-Zr-Nb High-Entropy Alloy Changes Hydrogen Sorption Properties

Abstract: Al0.10Ti0.30V0.25Zr0.10Nb0.25 was prepared to evaluate the effect of 10% aluminum into the previously reported quaternary alloy, Ti0.325V0.275Zr0.125Nb0.275. The as-cast quinary alloy formed a single-phase body centered cubic solid solution and transformed into a body centered tetragonal after hydrogenation. The alloy had a storage capacity of 1.6 H/M (2.6 wt.%) with fast absorption kinetics at room temperature, reaching full capacity within the first 10 min. The major improvements of Al addition (10%) were related to the desorption and cycling properties of the material. The temperature for hydrogen release was significantly decreased by around 100 °C, and the quinary alloy showed superior cycling stability and higher reversible storage capacity than its quaternary counterpart, 94% and 85% of their respective initial capacity, after 20 hydrogenation cycles without phase decomposition.
